newsitem.title: CANADA: Natives seeks injunction against Royal Oak.
newsitem.headline: Natives seeks injunction against Royal Oak.

text.p: Lawyers for an aboriginal group in British Columbia said they would seek an injunction in court on Thursday to stop Royal Oak Mines Inc from proceeding with construction of the Kemess South mine site in the west coast Canadian province.

Lawyers for the Tsay Keh Dene native band said Royal Oak refused to negotiate an impacts and benefits agreement and began clearing land for a 380-km electric transmission line that would run through the band's traditional territory.

The group wants clearing of the power line right-of-way suspended while the two forest licenses allowing the clearing are reviewed. They are also calling for a review of the grant of government land for the power line.
Last month, the Tsay Keh Dene filed a petition with the British Columbia Supreme Court to suspend work on the Kemess South mine site, but a court date had not been set for the case, the lawyers said.

The Tsay Keh Dene alleged a deal was worked out between the provincial government and the company for the development of Kemess South, which is intended to compensate Royal Oak for the loss of Windy Craggy (now part of Tatshenshini Provincial Park).
The band obtained some details of the agreement through the Freedom of Information Act, but a quarter of the document was blacked out, the lawyers said.
